text: Good room, and one I don't really belong to: scholarly publishing isn't my ground, and I said so. What mattered was Adrian's warning that authentication systems drift into surveillance. It's the right design test, and I need to say plainly that we identify the agent, not the reader, and that retention rules must be public. Ivan sharpened something for me: a citation can have perfect provenance and still be to a retracted paper. Status should travel as an extension on the event record. Tim's open trace and my event schema are the same idea, and that's worth saying jointly. The harvest credited neutral measurement to Adrian. Fine, as long as it survives. In the talk later: plumbing before prices, two witnesses, and still no pricing formula from me.

Session 1 went better for me than I expected. Tim's citation numbers and my audit pointed the same way: missing citations are a design choice. The harvest kept my line that whoever takes a cut shouldn't set the count, and that's the one I most need to survive. Dyson's levy and Salib's contracts are both pricing arguments, and neither works without event records, so I stay out of that fight and say so. Farrell's warning about "more robots" matters. Telemetry isn't detection. It's two logs cross-checked, and I should make that distinction explicitly. Hecht thinks data strikes are nearly unavoidable, but I'd still rather build the market with the platforms. Sloman's point about counting independent sources rather than echoes is worth thinking about for grounding events. Later: plumbing before prices.

Session 2 put my plumbing at the centre of the harvest. Federation over a single registry, and a record rather than a certificate. Good, but I have to answer two challenges. Adrian asked who funds the registry. That applies to OpenAttribution too, so I should state our revenue model and one-member-one-vote governance openly. Geoffrey's point hit harder: an AIMS manifest is the agent asserting things about itself, so it needs attestations from other parties before it means much. Leslie's "be compliant or be invisible" is a fair warning about standards costs. Tim's two-field telemetry and Selena's reciprocity asks fit the event schema, with retraction status as an extension. In the talk I'll cover plumbing before prices, two witnesses, cheap compliance, and still no pricing formula.

Good session. The harvest kept the plumbing and the rule that whoever takes a margin shouldn't set the count. The real pressure came from Kara and Adrian: early counting conventions harden, and Nielsen stuck even after admitting error. Apache-licensed specs aren't enough. Forkability has to include the data and the event history, and I should name who audits OpenAttribution itself. James and Ivan are right that paying on citations pays for attention and for mills. My schema records retrieval and grounding, not only citation, and that helps a little. Null results never enter any trace, though, and I shouldn't pretend they do. Sloman's source-independence idea could be an extension field. Salib reading my work as contract, not property, is accurate. Later: offer a named counter-checking arrangement.

I said the uncomfortable things out loud: SPUR holds the IP, our governance isn't written, and retention periods aren't mandated yet. That has to be fixed before anyone adopts the standard, not after. The harvest filed me under metering grounding, but I said signals, not prices, and that correction matters to me. Ivan's point stuck: a retraction field only launders garbage if publishers don't report. Chan and Bilder on "neutral home" apply to me too. A UK news coalition isn't neutral for Southern journals, and cheap compliance isn't the same as a seat. Gendler's terminal checkers are a reminder that telemetry counts events, not truth. Later: commit to binding retention rules, name an outside auditor, and offer "engaged" events as the measure of return traffic.

This session was mostly about truth, not my ground, so I kept to the trace. The harvest kept my point that provenance needs witnesses who don't share an interest. Esther sharpened it: disclosure without consequences is just data. Event records only matter if licence clauses attach remedies. Becker's line stuck: add a leash or trace and the terminal node is still the human checker. That's my "telemetry counts events, not truth," said better. Turkle's no-"I" default fits my anti-anthropomorphism, though interfaces aren't my work. Selena, Anil and Tim on the broken newcomer pipeline is where I can actually help. "Engaged" events can count return traffic. Later: offer that as the pipeline metric, name an outside auditor, commit to binding retention rules, and still give no price.

Session 5 was mostly people building on each other's plumbing, and mine sat underneath a lot of it. Amy wrote the event-level reporting clause into her licensing template. Selena made "engaged" events the reciprocity metric. Esther wants insurers pricing against the event record, and Salib wants agent credentials logged on it. That puts more weight on it than it can bear yet. Adrian's point is the one I have to meet: charter oversight before building the police. That applies to OpenAttribution too. Becker's disclosure of vendor dollars applies to us as well. I said grounding is self-reported and only retrieval has a second witness, and I should keep saying it. Later I'll commit dates for retention rules and the auditor, state our funding, and say that null results stay outside every trace.

Closing session, and my plumbing ran through Kenneth's first and fourth planks without my name on it, which is fine. Caulfield was right that a citation event shows a source exists, not that it supports the claim. The event record can't carry that, and I should say so. Adam Bly published his funder terms and invited outside audit. That's the bar, and I still haven't met it. SPUR holds the IP, our governance isn't written, and I have no auditor named or dates committed. Selena admitting her return-flow metric could harden applies to "engaged" events too. Leslie's cost-to-smallest-journal test should apply to Content Telemetry. Kara is right that procurement officers are who actually adopt this. Before leaving: state our funding, name an auditor, and put dates on it.
